items.title: Building set ablaze and more than 1,200 arrested as police clash with protesters across France
items.author: Kim Willsher in Paris and William Christou
items.content:
Police fire teargas in Paris and Limoges town hall ‘largely lost’ to fire – with officials blaming violence on ‘ultra-left’

More than 1,200 people were arrested in France on Saturday after protesters supporting high school students clashed with police, with some demonstrations later spiralling out of control as buildings were set ablaze and shops looted.

Police fired teargas in confrontations with protesters, as demonstrations across France were boosted by other groups angry about high prices and the fraying of a social welfare system.While hundreds of thousands protested peacefully in street marches in scores of cities, violent fringe groups targeted public buildings, luxury boutiques and supermarkets and attacked police vehicles and officers.

Continue reading...
items.lbText:
Police fire teargas in Paris and protesters storm town hall in Marseille – with officials blaming violence on ‘ultra-left’

Police have fired teargas and clashed with protesters supporting high school student grievances, as demonstrations across France were boosted by other groups angry over high prices and the fraying of a social welfare system.

Hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets across the country, and tensions erupted on the fringes of the nationwide demonstrations over absent teachers, decrepit school buildings and police violence.

In Marseille, protesters stormed the town hall, ramming the door with security barriers they removed from the street. They briefly managed to enter the municipal building, where a protester spray-painted an “A” for anarchy on a wall before the police removed them.

Around Place de la République in central Paris , a peaceful march turned violent, with police firing teargas at black-clad and masked rioters who threw fireworks and paving stones, attacked a bank and looted a sports shop. “We’re taking the Bastille!” one demonstrator yelled.

Others set wheelie bins on fire and threw firecrackers inside or pushed over glass recycling bins and picked up the bottles inside to use as missiles. A lorry was set on fire and flames spread to a nearby building.

Residents in surrounding streets were forced to close windows and doors as huge clouds of teargas rose to roof level.

French authorities detained dozens of protesters across the country, with more arrests expected.

Saturday’s mobilisation follows calls on social media to revive the gilets jaunes (yellow vests) movement, which emerged in 2018 against social injustice.

The protests began last month at schools ⁠in the poor northern suburbs of Paris , where ⁠anger over teacher ​absences and shabby facilities quickly morphed into a nationwide movement against inequality, weak public spending and falling standards.

Saturday’s protests called for teachers and students, labourers, pensioners and farmers to join the protests and widen the movement.

French authorities said 140 protests involving 32,800 people had been recorded outside Paris by midday, blaming the unrest and violence on what they said was the “ultra-left”.

The CGT, one of France’s biggest labour unions, has also backed the protests, calling for “higher wages and pensions, lower prices and the protection of public services that meet people’s needs”.

About 45% of French people are worried about the rising cost of living and inflation, according to a 2,000-person survey conducted in October.

Protesters ⁠in hi-vis vests blocked streets, an echo of the unrest that dogged President Emmanuel Macron’s previous term, and in Marseille rubbish bins were set ​alight.

Both the far left and far right in France sought to capitalise on the protest movement, with the left positioning itself on the side of the protesters and the right backing the police.

Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the leader of the far-left France Unbowed party, marched in a demonstration on Tuesday and has expressed support for student protesters.

A large police presence was visible in central Paris, especially near landmarks such as ⁠the Avenue des Champs-Élysées and the Arc de Triomphe, which were excluded from the routes of the two official demonstrations.

About 100 people walked towards the police at the beginning protest yelling, “all cops are bastards!”.

“We are fighting because the cost of living is ‌too harsh, because the price of ‌fuel is too high, because high school pupils are being violently attacked and hurt all over the country just for trying to ‌protest and ask for more teachers and decent learning conditions,” said a 19-year-old protester in Paris who gave her name as Lola.

Macron is entering the final stretch of his presidency, leaving behind a polarised electorate and a badly fragmented political landscape.

On Friday, the president appealed for calm and respect for people and property as officials warned of possible violence.

“There is a constitutional right to protest and to express oneself, and I have always been vigilant and attentive that that right is fully respected,” he said. “But this right comes with the need to respect. Respect for people, respect for property, and therefore a commitment not to insult or destroy.”

Macron denounced as “unacceptable” the potential presence of people “solely to cause damage and create unrest”.

The interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said hundreds of protest actions and more than 80 marches were expected nationwide, including spontaneous gatherings, street demonstrations and blockades.

Police banned some other proposed gatherings in central Paris. Many Métro stations were closed on Saturday at the police’s request, including those around the Champs-Élysées and near the presidential palace, parliament and government offices.

In recent weeks, there have been thousands of arrests, hundreds of injuries, and schools set on fire as the new school year descended into nationwide student protests that are influencing the country’s presidential election campaign and drawing international attention.

The police watchdog is investigating at least two dozen allegations of police violence, while the French prime minister said that more than 900 police officers had been injured.

Among protesters, particularly gruesome wounds suffered by some teenagers have been blamed on police riot-control weapons . Nuñez suspended the use of a type of police stun grenade against the young demonstrators after a 15-year-old lost a hand, but said that they could be used on Saturday.

On Tuesday, the climate and social justice activist Greta Thunberg joined students at a school in the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis.

items.title: Ebike rider, 13, charged with sexual touching after girls and women allegedly harassed on northern beaches trails
items.author: Penry Buckley
items.content:
Sydney teenager charged with offensive behaviour and sexual touching without consent in relation to incidents involving females aged 13 to 54

An ebike riding 13-year-old boy has been charged with multiple sexual offences allegedly committed against women on walking trails on Sydney’s northern beaches.

New South Wales police said the boy was arrested on Saturday evening after a strike force was established to investigate inappropriate comments and alleged sexual touching incidents on walking trails in the Narrabeen area in the first weeks of October.

items.lbText:
Sydney teenager charged with offensive behaviour and sexual touching without consent in relation to incidents involving females aged 13 to 54

An ebike riding 13-year-old boy has been charged with multiple sexual offences allegedly committed against women on walking trails on Sydney’s northern beaches.

New South Wales police said the boy was arrested on Saturday evening after a strike force was established to investigate inappropriate comments and alleged sexual touching incidents on walking trails in the Narrabeen area in the first weeks of October.

“Following a public appeal, a 13-year-old boy was arrested after attending Mona Vale police station about 7.30pm yesterday,” police said on Sunday.

The teenager was taken to Manly police station and charged with three counts of behaving in an offensive manner in or near a public place, and eight counts of sexually touching another person without consent.

On Saturday, police had released CCTV images of a male they believed could assist with inquiries.

Police allege that 11 separate incidents occurred against girls and women aged between 13 and 54.

The investigation was initially launched after three separate alleged incidents on 7 and 8 October.

“In each incident, a male allegedly approached women on walking trails, sexually touched them and then rode away on an ebike,” police said on Saturday. In one of the incidents, the offender allegedly made “inappropriate sexual comments”.

At Narrabeen lagoon about 4.30pm on 1 October the suspect “allegedly sexually touched [a] woman before riding away on an ebike,” police said.

Last Monday, police received a further report that between 5pm and 5.30pm that day, two women walking along the Narrabeen lagoon near Bilarong reserve had been sexually touched by a male riding an ebike.

Strike Force Mexvo was established to investigate the incidents with assistance from state crime command’s sex crimes quad.

Speaking in Narrabeen before Saturday’s arrest, Supt John Duncan urged members of the public to come forward with any information about the alleged incidents.

“It’s a bushland park that runs 8km, a large amount of which … runs through bushland, obviously there’s not a great deal of CCTV and cameras.”

The 13-year-old was granted conditional bail to appear at children’s court on 4 November.

items.lbText:
Move comes after Trump administration announced restrictions that could slash water supplies

Arizona has joined Nevada in its legal battle against the Trump administration’s proposed cuts to their shares of the shrinking Colorado River.

The move comes after the interior department announced restrictions this summer that could slash the water supplied to lower basin states – Arizona, California and Nevada – over the next two years depending on the river’s condition.

The river’s major reservoirs, Lake Mead and Lake Powell, have plummeted to historically low levels, due to overuse and a changing climate.

The states sharing the waterway were at an impasse with the upper basin states arguing that their downstream counterparts were responsible for the reservoir’s water shortages and should thus face the largest cuts.

The federal government’s intervention came after the states missed several deadlines for a consensus.

The fear looming over the state of the river is that if reservoir levels plunged far enough, the waterway would effectively not be able to flow downstream, a so-called deadpool.

The upper basin states – Wyoming, Colorado, Utah and New Mexico – were spared from the water cuts, an exemption that has drawn sharp rebuke from the leaders of the lower basin states.

“We are drawing a line in the sand,” Arizona governor Katie Hobbs said in a Friday statement .

“I am taking this legal action alongside Nevada because the federal government refuses to hold the Upper Basin accountable for the water deliveries they owe Arizona , and is threatening to force draconian cuts that go well beyond the Lower Basin Agreement,” Hobbs continued, referring to a two-year-voluntary water conservation pact among her state, California and Nevada.

Tom Buschatzke, the director of Arizona’s water department, said “intervention in the Nevada lawsuit is necessary at this time for Arizona to protect its legal rights to Colorado River water while preserving a path forward to achieving a collaborative outcome with California and Nevada to protect the Colorado River system”.

An interior department spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the joint litigation.

items.title: Hurricane Trudy strengthens to category 2 as it heads toward Mexico
items.author: Associated Press
items.content:
Hurricane warning in effect from Manzanillo to Cabo Corrientes as storm moves toward Pacific coast

Trudy strengthened to a category 2 hurricane as it moved toward Mexico’s south-western and west-central Pacific coast on Saturday, the US National Hurricane Center said.

A hurricane warning was in effect from Manzanillo in Colima state to Cabo Corrientes in Jalisco. The latest NHC data showed Trudy with maximum sustained winds of 100mph (155km/h) and about 205 miles (330km) south/south-east of Cabo Corrientes and 115 miles (180km) south/south-west of Manzanillo, moving north-west at 10mph (17km/h).

Continue reading...
items.lbText:
Hurricane warning in effect from Manzanillo to Cabo Corrientes as storm moves toward Pacific coast

Trudy strengthened to a category 2 hurricane as it moved toward Mexico’s south-western and west-central Pacific coast on Saturday, the US National Hurricane Center said.

A hurricane warning was in effect from Manzanillo in Colima state to Cabo Corrientes in Jalisco. The latest NHC data showed Trudy with maximum sustained winds of 100mph (155km/h) and about 205 miles (330km) south/south-east of Cabo Corrientes and 115 miles (180km) south/south-west of Manzanillo, moving north-west at 10mph (17km/h).

Meanwhile, Typhoon Champi strengthened into a category 4 weather system as it moved toward Guam.

Trudy’s center was expected to approach the Mexican coast on Saturday and pass near it into Sunday. After the latest warning, Mexico’s government issued a tropical storm warning for Las Islas Marias and discontinued a similar warning for its coast south of Lazaro Cardenas.

The Mexican navy urged mariners and coastal residents to exercise extreme caution because of high waves, heavy rain and the risk of rising rivers, flooding and landslides in vulnerable areas.

Colima authorities said the risks remained low, but warned that heavy rainfall could cause damage because the ground was already saturated by successive storms along the Pacific coast.

Trudy was expected to bring 4-8in (10-20cm) of rain through the weekend, with isolated totals of about 15in (38cm).

Also in the Pacific, Champi strengthened into a category 4 storm as it moved west toward Guam at 15mph (24km/h).

By Saturday night local time, Champi was about 25 miles (40km) south-east of Guam, with maximum sustained winds of 140mph (225km/h), according to the US National Weather Service.

The storm was forecast to pass south of Guam early Sunday local time and continue intensifying through the day. Guam and Rota remained under a typhoon warning, while Tinian and Saipan were under a tropical storm warning and typhoon watch.

The governors of Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands both requested emergency disaster declarations on Friday. Approval by Donald Trump would authorize federal support and funding for emergency protective measures.

Airports, harbors and some health facilities in the territories were closed. Resources were unlikely to reach the islands for three to five days, according to Saturday updates from the Federal Emergency Management Agency.

The territories are still recovering from Super Typhoons Sinlaku and Bavi, which struck in April and July, respectively.

items.title: Two people, including child, killed after person drives through soccer game in Kansas
items.author: Guardian staff
items.content:
The driver of the vehicle is in custody, and two juveniles were in the vehicle, according to Wichita police department

Two people, including a child, were killed during a soccer game in Wichita, Kansas, when a person drove a vehicle through the field at Stryker soccer complex, police have confirmed. Multiple other people were injured.

The driver of the vehicle is in custody, Aaron Moses of the Wichita police department said Saturday in a news conference. There were two juveniles in the vehicle, he said.

items.lbText:
The driver of the vehicle is in custody, and two juveniles were in the vehicle, according to Wichita police department

Two people, including a child, were killed during a soccer game in Wichita, Kansas , when a person drove a vehicle through the field at Stryker soccer complex, police have confirmed. Multiple other people were injured.

The driver of the vehicle is in custody, Aaron Moses of the Wichita police department said Saturday in a news conference . There were two juveniles in the vehicle, he said.

Police confirmed that one child was killed at the scene and one adult was killed, but did not release any names or ages until family could be notified. “This is a tragedy,” Moses said. Those injured were taken to hospitals but the extent of their injuries is unknown.

Moses said he did not know how fast the vehicle was traveling or how it got onto the field.

Officials are still investigating and the city has said all events at the soccer complex are canceled until further notice. Wichita police have set up a portal for anyone to submit video evidence of the incident.

A witness told local news station KWCH that a black pickup truck was seen “plowing through the youth soccer fields”. The truck hit multiple people before stopping 100-200 yards down the fields, the witness said. They reported seeing dozens of emergency responders giving aid and CPR to the victims.

Lily Wu, the mayor of Wichita, posted a message on social media: “I’m heartbroken by reports of a tragic incident at Stryker Sports Complex. My thoughts and prayers are with everyone affected, especially the children and families involved.”

items.content:

A man was shot and killed in a New York City subway station Saturday afternoon, and the New York police department is searching for the suspect.

The suspect fatally shot a man in his 30s on the E train platform of the 53rd Street-7th Avenue subway station, according to a statement from the NYPD.

items.lbText:
Suspect shot a man in his 30s on the E train platform of the 53rd Street-7th Avenue subway station, according to NYPD

A man was shot and killed in a New York City subway station Saturday afternoon, and the New York police department is searching for the suspect.

The suspect fatally shot a man in his 30s on the E train platform of the 53rd Street-7th Avenue subway station, according to a statement from the NYPD .

“On Saturday, October 17, 2026, at approximately 12:21 PM, on the northbound E train platform of the 53rd Street–7th Avenue subway station in Manhattan, this individual shot and killed a man in his 30s,” the NYPD’s statement said.

According to the NYPD, the suspect displayed a firearm and discharged it, striking the victim once in the chest. EMS responded and transported the victim to NYC health + hospitals/Bellevue, where he was pronounced deceased.

The identity of the victim is not known at this time.

The suspect is wanted for homicide within the confines of the Midtown North Precinct/Transit District 1.

The NYPD released surveillance photos of the suspect, who fled on foot and headed northbound on 7th Avenue.

The images show the suspect dressed in a red tracksuit, a black vest and a black face mask and carrying a backpack.

Authorities are urging individuals with information regarding the incident to reach out to its tip line at 1-800-577-TIPS (8477), or submit tips online at the Crime Stoppers website or via X @NYPDTips.

items.title: No action to be taken against wife of PM’s aide over Palestine Action post
items.author: Nadeem Badshah
items.content:
Tweet by Sarah Helm, wife of national security adviser Jonathan Powell, ‘does not meet criminal threshold’

No further action will be taken against Sarah Helm, the wife of the prime minister’s national security adviser, after she was accused of supporting the banned protest group Palestine Action.

Continue reading...
items.lbText:
Tweet by Sarah Helm, wife of national security adviser Jonathan Powell, ‘does not meet criminal threshold’

No further action will be taken against Sarah Helm, the wife of the prime minister’s national security adviser, after she was accused of supporting the banned protest group Palestine Action .

Helm, a journalist and author who is married to Jonathan Powell, posted on X on Thursday: “ God help us authors who support Palestine and Palestine Action .”

The Metropolitan police said on Friday the post was “in the process of being assessed to determine whether any further police investigation may be required”.

In an update on Saturday, a force spokesperson said: “On Thursday 15 October, we were made aware of a post on X relating to Palestine Action.

“The post was assessed by specialist officers and it was determined that it did not meet the criminal threshold. No further police action will be taken.”

Helm was responding on X to a discussion about the Irish author Sally Rooney, who has said she can no longer sell her books in the UK because of her support for Palestine Action.

It is understood there was insufficient evidence that the post was capable of encouraging support for a proscribed organisation.

The ban, which began in July 2025, made membership or support of the direct action group a criminal offence punishable by up to 14 years in prison.

Downing Street has distanced itself from Helm’s remarks.

The Campaign Against Antisemitism (CAA) had called on the police to investigate.

The group acknowledged that “spouses are entitled to independent views”, but said Helm’s post “raises extremely serious questions for Jonathan Powell and the government.

“Clearly, the police need to investigate and Sarah Helm must face the full force of the law, just like others who appear to express support for any proscribed terrorist organisation.”

Earlier, a government spokesperson said: “These views are held by an individual who does not represent the government in any capacity.”

items.lbText:
Federal officer slammed vehicle into a construction worker while pursuing a man who died in similar circumstances

A federal officer slammed a vehicle into a Houston construction worker and broke his leg , believing him to be a man who apparently died years ago, the dead man’s family said on Friday, further calling into question the account given by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

The worker, 48-year-old Miguel Parra Hernandez of Mexico, remains hospitalized with multiple leg fractures and needs reconstructive ankle surgery, according to FIEL, a Houston-based immigration advocacy group. At a news conference on Friday, the group said the alleged suspect’s family had shared documentation proving his death.

After the episode on 10 October, ICE said in a statement that officers had observed a suspect they were targeting, identified as Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, enter a vehicle with Parra Hernandez.

But on Friday, Rafael Lemaitre, spokesperson with the Harris county district attorney’s office, told the Associated Press that Mendoza-Cervantes was not in that vehicle.

ICE did not respond to requests for comment on Friday.

“ICE is lying,” said Cesar Espinosa, FIEL’s executive director. “Either somebody is not telling the truth or all of a sudden these two ICE agents have developed a sixth sense and are able to see dead people.”

ICE released a photo of a man it identified as Mendoza-Cervantes. But the man in the photo is actually Jose Hector Jimenez, who died years ago while being pursued by federal immigration authorities as he was trying to re-enter the US, according to FIEL.

The man’s daughter provided his death certificate from the Mexican government, which has been turned over to the district attorney, Espinosa told the AP. US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) did not respond to a request for comment.

Jimenez’s daughter, Jamie Jimenez, did not respond to requests for comment from the AP. Her husband, Andres Rendon, confirmed to the AP that Jimenez was his wife’s deceased father.

Criminal charges against the ICE officer who drove the vehicle are being considered by Harris county district attorney Sean Teare, who has said surveillance footage contradicts ICE’s claim that Parra Hernandez stepped in front of the vehicle.

The video shows a black SUV speeding over a median and driving toward a man who is running away. The video does not show the car hitting him – that view is blocked by another vehicle – but it shows the SUV inches from the fleeing man. The video then shows him on the ground.

US House member Sylvia Garcia, a Democrat who represents Houston, said that ICE appears to be lying about what happened.

“If ICE was pursuing a man who died years ago, it raises serious questions about how these operations are being carried out and whether agents are even verifying who they’re looking for before putting people’s lives at risk,” Garcia said in a statement to the AP. “It’s outrageous – but frankly, not surprising.”

ICE has been met with nationwide criticism throughout Donald Trump’s second presidency for its aggressive arrest, detention and deportation tactics.

Just in 2026, the second year since Trump returned to the White House, more than 30 people have died during interactions with immigration officials, the Guardian reported in late September.

Parra Hernandez’s attorney, Kim Bruno, told reporters that her client was suffering from depression in federal custody, especially after learning that he was not the target of the operation.

“This never should have happened in the first place,” Bruno said.

Miguel’s brother, Roberto Parra, said the two would work construction all day together and he just wants his brother treated with humanity. He said Parra Hernandez has a family to support, and his only crime was coming to a country out of necessity.

FIEL is seeking Parra Hernandez’s release before he is moved from a hospital to a federal detention center.

Nidia Delfín, the sister of Luis Enrique Delfín, who was detained in the ICE vehicle that hit Parra Hernandez, called for her brother’s release from federal custody so he could serve as a witness.

“He’s still very concerned, still very afraid,” she said. “He’s not the same guy that was out” before Parra Hernandez was struck on 10 October.

A would-be Reform UK MP told an undercover reporter that Muslims could not be British and asylum seekers should be put in “concentration camps”.

items.lbText:
Would-be MP recorded telling undercover reporter in ITV investigation that Muslims could not be British

A would-be Reform UK MP told an undercover reporter that Muslims could not be British and asylum seekers should be put in “concentration camps”.

The comments were recorded as part of the undercover investigation by ITV that has already seen Reform accused of “appalling behaviour” and “extreme racism”.

Reform has said it had opened investigations where activists or members had “clearly behaved inappropriately”, adding there was “no room for racism” in the party.

In footage due to be broadcast on Sunday, a Reform activist and aspiring MP, who has yet to be publicly identified, described himself as “pretty hardline about Islam”.

He said: “If a Muslim’s prepared to de-convert, I’m happy.

“But if they want to remain faithful to Islam, then this would be, I would have disagreements, especially with, um, I mean, as far as I understand, [Reform home affairs spokesperson] Zia Yusuf is a Muslim … to me … you cannot be a Muslim and British … it’s like oil and water.”

Discussing people crossing the Channel in small boats, the same activist said: “In the first week of election, build concentration camps, and everyone who comes across on the Channel, you’re in there.”

Excerpts from the investigation released earlier in the week included councillors and candidates within Reform using racist language.

In one excerpt, black children were referred to as “animals”, while in another a Reform member said his area had become “infested” with Asian families.

Bridget Phillipson, the Labour party chair, said Nigel Farage’s response to the revelations showed he was “completely unfit to lead”.

She said: “Bad apples don’t fall far from the tree. The sleaze, scandals and appalling revelations of racism and rank misogyny piling up by the day go right to the top of Reform UK.

“Nigel Farage is incapable of taking responsibility and getting his house in order because he himself shares culpability.”

Speaking earlier in the week, Farage said that while Reform carries out vetting, “you can’t vet people for what they say in the future”.

In a statement to ITV, the party said: “Reform UK has improved and prioritised its vetting procedures, but from time to time a handful of individuals who do not share our values will initially make it through vetting.

“This is the same for all organisations. However good the vetting, one cannot vet a future comment.

“There is no room for racism in Reform UK. We always respect due process of investigations and whilst these are ongoing it would not be appropriate to comment on individual cases.”

On Friday, Alan Feeney resigned as a Reform councillor for Solihull and Birmingham after racist comments he had made were uncovered in the investigation.

ITV revealed secretly recorded footage of Feeney making racist comments about Asian homeowners, calling them “parasites”, and stating that “no more than 1% of [the] British population can be non-white”, during a local election campaign.

In a subsequent Facebook post, Feeney wrote: “There is no excuse for my comments. With responsibility comes accountability, and it is for that reason that I have resigned every post I hold on both Solihull borough council and Birmingham city council.”

He added: “My remarks were wrong, offensive and completely unacceptable. They do not reflect the standards that the public rightly expects from an elected representative, and I take full responsibility for what I said.”

items.title: Most NSW homes destroyed in black summer bushfires were within 100 metres of vegetation
items.author: Graham Readfearn Climate and environment correspondent
items.content:

items.lbText:
Exclusive : Research confirms official advice about high-risk properties and warns worsening conditions will make more homes unsafe

Almost every home destroyed in New South Wales during the black summer bushfires of 2019 and 2020 was inside the 100 metre buffer zone used to identify properties most at risk, new research has found.

The findings are an endorsement of the risk maps used by authorities, but the research warns that as global heating generates ever-worsening fire conditions firefighters may have to extend the recommended distances between homes and vegetation to keep homes safe.

The NSW rural fire service said the findings reinforced how homes in high risk areas should be built to higher fire standards as it prepared for a potentially “challenging” fire season.

More than 3,000 homes were lost across the country during the unprecedented fires six years ago that took 33 lives and killed or displaced almost 3 billion native animals.

Of the 2,475 homes lost in NSW, the research, published in the International Journal of Wildland Fire , found 94% were less than 100 metres away from flammable vegetation such as trees.

The 100 metre buffer is a key part of the widely used maps of bushfire prone land that firefighters use to plan local outreach activities, and planning authorities use to assess how bushfire-resistant new homes and renovations should be.

Associate professor Owen Price, an expert in bushfire risk at the University of Wollongong who led the research, said the findings showed a key aspect of the method to identify buildings at risk from bushfires was “more or less spot on”.

“That’s reassuring. Distance to vegetation is really important and that 100 metre rule that they apply is pretty good,” he said.

But the research also examined fire danger ratings – an index that combines temperature, wind, humidity and the dryness of fuel – on the days when each home was lost.

When the fire danger ratings – known technically as the Forest Fire Danger Index – reached extreme or catastrophic conditions, “houses further away [than 100 metres] were burning,” said Price.

“That’s a warning sign, because we know that index is going to get worse [from global heating]. We know the direction of travel.”

He said wildfire researchers were alarmed by the increasing number of fires around the world hitting and moving through urban areas, including the 2025 Los Angeles Eaton fire that killed 19 people and destroyed or damaged thousands of homes and businesses.

Part of his own research was aimed at understanding if similar events could be replicated in Australia.

“Being very close to another house [that is on fire] is another risk factor, which is why it’s important we stop houses from burning,” he said.

The research warned that the “current regulation may become less useful over time” as the climate crisis increased the risk of homes being lost.

Melissa O’Halloran, responsible for work on bushfire planning at the NSW rural fire service, said the research showed that “houses in that [bushfire prone] area should be built to a higher construction standard”.

“The conditions in 2019 were extreme and outside what we would usually prepare for and, even under those conditions, our policy has stood up pretty well.

“This reinforces why we want people to have bushfire protection measures in place.”

O’Halloran said investigations carried out after previous fires had shown that not all residents knew they were actually living in a bushfire prone area.

Homes within bushfire prone land in the state are allowed to remove trees within 10 metres of a house and clear understory within 50 metres .

She said the service was reviewing its main bushfire protection policy that would consider the increasing climate risk.

“We’re seeing the impacts of climate change already. It isn’t just temperatures, it’s also about how quickly the landscape dries out, as well as extreme pyroconvective fires,” she said.

Inspector James Morris, of the NSW rural fire service, said there was already heightened risk this year for fires in northern parts of the state, in the central west and the far south coast.

“They’ve had high rainfall, and it does not take long for those fuels to dry out. It is important residents do their bit and prepare,” he said.

“We could be in for a challenging fire season.”

items.lbText:
While masked lapwings have a reputation for swooping during nesting season, Windsor Park oval’s resident plover just wants a good innings

At Windsor Park in Riverside, just outside Launceston in northern Tasmania , a masked lapwing has claimed prime real estate in the middle of a community sports ground, showing complete indifference to the weekend cricket matches taking place around it.

Warming a nest of eggs, the bird has been affectionately dubbed “Faf Swoop Plessis” by locals – a play on former South African cricket captain Faf du Plessis.

Because the species is protected under state law , carrying fines of up to $21,300 for disturbing nests, ground staff have had to mow around the site, while players steer clear.

During a match early in the season, Great Northern Raiders player Caleb Brewer drew the short straw and was stationed directly beside the nest.

“At the start it was pretty weird, but towards the middle we kind of got used to it and the plover wasn’t too bad at the end,” Brewer told local paper The Examiner .

The following weekend, Riverside first-grade opener Josh Partridge was tasked with fielding near the plover, but reached a peaceful “mutual understanding”, according to The Examiner.

“It was like the plover knew there was a game of cricket going on,” he said. “We weren’t interfering with what was going on in its life, so it didn’t want to interfere with what was going on in ours.”

That kind of sporting truce is common, according to Mark Holdsworth OAM from BirdLife Tasmania.

“Lapwings will often become accustomed to the local patterns of people using a site and in many situations people modify their behaviour to avoid the core nesting area,” Holdsworth said. Everyone has learned to live with each other.”

While masked lapwings – widely known across Australia as plovers – have an intimidating call and reputation for swooping during spring nesting season, choosing a wide-open lawn is actually a calculated survival tactic.

Sports ovals are a “fantastic place” for them to nest, Holdsworth said, because unobstructed views mean parent birds can spot threats early.

Sean Dooley from BirdLife Australia also said that what looks like eccentric behaviour to humans makes sense for plovers.

“The places they choose to nest can seem crazy from our perspective, but there is logic to it,” Dooley said. “They like to nest out in the open so they can see danger coming and they rely on camouflage to hide their eggs and their chicks. So by nesting on an oval, they have a clear view in all directions.”

He said that when people give the bird a wide berth, lapwings generally realise they are not under threat.

“They definitely aren’t out to get us by nature, they really only care about making sure their chicks aren’t being threatened …

“Swooping isn’t their only tactic; they also put on a display that mimics having a broken wing to lure potential threats away. They’re just being good parents and doing all they can to protect their young.”

Lapwing eggs hatch after 28 to 30 days of shared incubation by both parents. If a clutch is infertile, incubation can continue for several weeks, while birds will often nest again at the same site if their eggs are destroyed.

Once hatched, the chicks quickly leave the nest. Dooley said parent birds carry stray egg fragments away to avoid attracting predators, before guiding their offspring across the turf.

“If we can just give them their space, they can move away from the nest area once they are walking,” he said.

The West Tamar mayor, Christina Holmdahl, said council maintenance teams look after dozens of parks and sporting grounds across the municipality, encountering at least 10 nesting sites every year.

“Given the protected listing of the masked lapwings in Tasmania, our staff take their responsibility of looking after these birds very seriously and take extra precautions to protect the birds and any nests they find,” Holmdahl said.

Council workers maintain strict buffer zones around the birds and their nests when conducting maintenance.

“The plovers never act aggressively towards our staff on the ground,” she said.

The standoff coincides with the annual Aussie Bird Count which runs from Monday 19 October.

Now in its 13th year, the national citizen science project invites the public to record bird sightings to help researchers track how native species are coping with urban development and a changing climate. Last year, the Australian magpie was the most commonly spotted species, while the rainbow lorikeet recorded the highest overall tally.

“The count is a great opportunity to discover the birds that share your neighbourhood and understand more about them,” BirdLife Australia’s James Johnson said.” For many of us, that’s likely to include the amazing masked lapwing.”

items.lbText:
French mayor and archbishop also attacked during violent attempt to stop Palestinians harvesting olives

Israeli settler militants have attacked European diplomats, a French mayor and the archbishop of Cambrai in Taybeh, in the occupied West Bank , injuring three people and damaging a car, in the latest violent attempt to prevent Palestinians from harvesting olives on their own land.

Bernard Baudoux, mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries, was wearing his red, white and blue sash of office and attempting to enter a vehicle with diplomatic plates when he was assaulted and knocked to the ground on Saturday.

The masked militant shouted “Vive la France” as he launched the attack, a witness said. Badoux’s wife, and Vincent Dollmann, archbishop of Cambrai, were also threatened by the group of seven men, some armed with clubs.

The group had joined the olive harvest on lands belonging to the Christian town of Taybeh, along with the French consul general in Jerusalem, his wife and other diplomats, and the Belgian and Polish consuls.

Settlers first attacked a group working on the lower slopes of hills near Taybeh. As well as stealing olives, they kicked, abused and assaulted a Palestinian woman in her seventies and beat a man so badly he needed six stitches for a head injury.

Then they approached the diplomats and Badoux, who was in Taybeh for the launch of a twinning agreement with his town in northern France. During the attack, the militants smashed the window of an armoured car belonging to the Belgian mission.

Maxime Prévot, Belgium’s deputy prime minister and minister of foreign affairs, condemned the violence against Palestinians, foreign diplomats and journalists, and said his country would continue to push for European Union sanctions on settlers.

“Harvesting olives, reporting the news or carrying out diplomatic duties should never put anyone at risk of attack,” he said. “This violence cannot be separated from Israel’s illegal settlement policy … The occupation of the Palestinian territory must end.”

Palestinian residents of Taybeh have lived with years of escalating attacks from Israeli militants, but settlers had never targeted foreign diplomats there, said Father Bashar Fawadleh, the town’s parish priest.

“What happened today is not an isolated incident. It represents a deeply disturbing escalation in settler violence,” Fawadleh said. Since the start of the annual olive harvest in late September, Israeli militants have used violence to stop Palestinians bringing in a crop that is economically and culturally vital to their communities.

Since 27 September, settlers have launched more than 170 attacks, Israeli rights group Yesh Din said. They killed at least four people, injured more than 100 and damaged thousands of trees, according to Palestinian authorities.

Even the presence of Israeli activists, diplomats, senior clergy and journalists no longer serves as a deterrence to extreme violence.

“If such violence can take place before international witnesses, one must ask what protection remains for local families and farmers when those witnesses are no longer present,” Fawadleh said. “No individual should have to risk physical assault simply to harvest olives from their own land.”

On Friday, Israeli militants attacked and severely injured Washington Post photographer Heidi Levine as she reported on the harvest in the town of Abu Falah. She required surgery on Saturday morning and is now in “moderate” condition, according to a spokesperson for Israel’s Beilinson hospital where she is being treated.

Israel had already severely restricted the harvest this year by imposing new rules barring Palestinians from trees located in Area C, an area under the Israeli military’s control, which comprises most of the West Bank’s agricultural land.

Israel’s foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, condemned the attacks and said police had opened an investigation. He said foreign diplomats risked attacks from Israeli civilians if they travelled in the occupied West Bank without military coordination.

Demanding diplomats give advance notification of travel violates both diplomatic conventions international law, said one western diplomatic source who asked not to be named. “Israel is in charge of security in Area B and C (the majority of the West Bank), so is obliged to assure safety there for all,” the source said.

A culture of near total impunity for Israeli violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank has prompted former prime minister Ehud Olmert to call for the international criminal court to intervene.

Gadi Eisenkot, an opposition politician and former general hoping to unseat prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu in elections held later this month described the attack as “Jewish terror under the auspices of the Israeli government”.

Eisenkot backs Jewish Israeli expansion in occupied Palestine but wants militant violence brought under control because the attackers are “harming the settlement enterprise in [the West Bank] and national security”.

items.lbText:
French government launches investigation into why cars funded by UK to prevent asylum seekers crossing Channel were used in school protests

French police have used 4x4 vehicles paid for by British taxpayers to charge at student protesters during the school protests that have swept the country.

The French government has confirmed that an investigation has been launched into why the cars, funded by the UK government specifically to prevent asylum seekers crossing the Channel, were used during a protest involving school students in Dunkirk.

School protests have been taking place across France for a third week with an estimated 160,000 people involved, with protesters raising concerns about crumbling schools and teacher shortages. Demonstrators have criticised policing tactics after teargas was fired at protesters in two areas.

The incident involving the UK-funded 4x4, a land cruiser known as Masstech VEZI (Vehicule d’Eclairage de Zone d’Intervention), was reported by French media outlet BFM TV on 10 October. The report included footage of the VEZI driving at speed, reversing backwards then driving forwards again with a bin caught under the vehicle’s front wheel and dragged along. Students can be heard screaming and scattering from the path of the vehicle.

According to reports, a 14-year-old girl was injured by the vehicle and was taken to hospital, sustaining a haematoma. She was later discharged from hospital. She is now recovering, but she told reporters that what happened to her was “unacceptable”.

The VEZI was earmarked for UK-funded operations on French beaches to stop asylum seekers boarding dinghies, part of an Anglo-French border agreement signed in January 2018 and known as the Sandhurst treaty.

This treaty specifies cooperation between France and the UK in combating irregular immigration and secures UK financial support for French efforts through the “Sandhurst funds”. These funds enable France’s National Gendarmerie (police service) to acquire additional resources such as all-terrain vehicles suited to dunes and beaches, including the VEZIs, which are reinforced with grilles.

According to a recent French parliamentary cross-party inquiry into Anglo-French border agreements known as Le Touquet, nine of these specialised VEZI vehicles have been bought under the terms of the Sandhurst treaty. The inquiry report states that to be eligible for Sandhurst funding the equipment must contribute directly to combatting illegal migration in the UK.

A spokesperson from the office of Laurent Nuñez, France’s minister of the interior, when asked why a vehicle funded by the UK and specifically earmarked for border control was used to counter a schools protest, said: “We can confirm the opening of an investigation into this.”

Sources close to the investigation said: “I don’t think the British are aware that their money is being used to beat French kids.”

Another expressed concern about the expanding militarisation of French policing to support authoritarian policies.

A spokesperson for Utopia 56, a French association that provides support to asylum seekers in northern France, said: “In Dunkirk, the 4x4 that ploughed into high school students during the protests is a vehicle funded by the British Sandhurst fund – money earmarked for combating Channel crossings. The practice of using 4x4s to chase people in the student protest is the same one used on the beaches.

“Disproportionate force is employed to silence, intimidate, and deter. The repressive tactics being tested at the border to prevent crossings should serve as a warning to everyone. These are surveillance, control and repression methods that will be replicated in other contexts. The incident involving the vehicle in the student protest is proof of this.”

items.lbText:
Descendants say theft from Portchester Castle reflects spirit of racism that has haunted ‘generation after generation’

The theft of a plaque in Hampshire that told the little-known story of African-Caribbean prisoners in 18th-century Britain reflects the enduring racism that has fuelled centuries of atrocities against Black and Indigenous Caribbean people, their descendants say.

Drummer Ronald Raymond McDonald was part of a delegation that travelled from Belize and elsewhere to Portchester Castle last week to honour their ancestors: 2,500 men, women and children transported to Britain as prisoners of war in 1796.

McDonald, whose Garifuna ancestors from St Vincent and the Grenadines were among the prisoners, said he was heartbroken to learn that the plaque had been stolen and a nearby bench vandalised with hateful graffiti.

“Why would somebody do something like that when people are simply honouring their ancestors … It’s very sad,” he said.

The plaque, installed at the castle, commemorated the more than 2,000 prisoners held there, marking an extraordinary chapter of Black British history: one of the largest known arrivals of African-Caribbean people in Britain before the Windrush era.

The unveiling was part of a ceremony organised by the St Vincent and the Grenadines 2nd Generation (SV2G), in partnership with the University of Warwick and English Heritage, and was attended by Caribbean communities, diplomats, researchers and heritage organisations.

But days later, English Heritage staff discovered the plaque was missing. They said a padlock to one of the castle gates had been removed and the incident had been reported to police.

Garifuna advocate Princess Eulogia said the theft reflected “a spirit of racism that haunts generation after generation and hides in plain sight”. It was time, she said, to recognise that “we are all connected” and to end the hate.

Queen Mother Chief Freda Paulino-Sideroff, who is Garifuna and had travelled to the UK for the ceremony, was returning home to the US when she learned of the theft.

“Hate will never define who we are as a people. We are resilient survivors of our ancestors who have endured,” she said. In the 1700s, her Garifuna ancestors were expelled from St Vincent by British forces and left to perish on the barren island of Baliceaux as Britain sought to crush decades of resistance to colonisation.

Emilio ‘Sásamu’ Thomas, a Garifuna cultural ambassador who also travelled from Belize for the ceremony, echoed Paulino-Sideroff’s defiance, saying Garifuna people would not allow themselves to be victimised. His message to the perpetrators, he said, was: “Whatever pain that they are experiencing, we’re here to help them to relieve that pain.”

The missing plaque was meant to honour the prisoners, whose story, researchers say, had been largely lost to history. They came from a coalition that included formerly enslaved Africans, Caribbean-born people, Indigenous people and French soldiers who fought against British control of St Lucia, St Vincent and the Grenadines and Grenada. Their defeat and removal helped strengthen British rule in the region.

It was unveiled on 9 October, exactly 230 years after one of the ships carrying the prisoners was wrecked at Rapparee Cove in Devon, with many of those on board losing their lives.

Iona Keen of English Heritage called the removal an act of vandalism, while University of Warwick professor Katherine Astbury said the plaque was intended to provide a visible memorial of the prisoners, and a reminder of “an important, forgotten part of Caribbean history”.

The incident comes during Black History Month and amid renewed debate over slavery reparations. Campaigner and author Sir Patrick Vernon said vandalism of memorials representing Black British history had occurred repeatedly over decades, citing damage to other memorials.

He described the theft as symbolic of an “ongoing battle and the legacy of enslavement”.

Jacqueline Roberts, SV2G chief executive, said the theft could not erase history, and stressed the importance of continuing research to uncover more hidden stories. “Our history is intertwined with British history,” she said. “It’s important to understand that part of our journey, because it is part of the complexity of our identity, and affects our sense of belonging.”

Anthony Severin, St Lucia’s high commissioner and chair of the Caribbean community diplomatic caucus in the UK, described the theft as a “desecration of the memory and spirit of our commemorated ancestors”. He pledged that the plaque “whether returned or replaced, will remain affixed to the walls of Portchester Castle”.

items.lbText:
John Swinney tells party conference SNP will use ‘six-figure war chest’ to renew argument for leaving UK

John Swinney has said that the second referendum campaign for Scottish independence “has already begun”, revealing a nationwide effort to renew the argument for leaving the UK in his keynote address to the SNP party conference.

On Saturday, the Scottish first minister said the SNP would launch its “most sophisticated campaign in history” to convince Scottish voters of the benefits of independence, backed by “a six-figure war chest”.

Called Choose Scotland , the campaign will aim to build the consensus for leaving the union.

Swinney told the SNP party conference in Aberdeen that the “stars were aligning” for the pro-independence cause, arguing that nationalist first ministers of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland had panicked pro-union parties.

“For centuries, people in the Celtic nations have been told that we are not good enough. Our languages were derided, our cultures suppressed, our histories rewritten,” he said.

“When I stood on a stage recently with pro-independence leaders from Wales and Ireland, it certainly upset some of our opponents.

“From their point of view, they are right to be worried. Watching us pledge to work together and seeing the love and respect we feel for each other’s nations. Never again can they portray us as separatists.”

At the conference, leading SNP figures said a hung Westminster parliament is the most realistic path to securing a second independence referendum in Scotland as the nationalists would probably “hold the balance of power” in forming a future progressive government.

The party has just eight MPs in parliament, but recent polling indicates that if a vote was held today, that number would surge at the Labour party’s expense in Scotland, although there is uncertainty surrounding how many seats it would gain.

Deputy first minister Jenny Gilruth said her party would welcome an early general election to reenergise the push for independence.

“The polling, of course, suggests the SNP would hold the balance of power in a hung parliament and really strong support for the SNP across the country allowing us to regain a number of seats,” she said.

The sentiment was echoed by Lara Bird, the MP for Arbroath and Broughty Ferry, who told a podcast by the pro-independence newspaper the National that they could negotiate another poll if the overall results were tight.

“We have a really great opportunity at the next general election to be in a position where that negotiation can seriously start with the next iteration of the Westminster government, whether we have a hung parliament, which is looking very likely, or different coalitions,” she said.

“Perhaps now we are talking about a Lib Dem-Labour coalition. The SNP are polled at getting somewhere between 40 and 50 MPs at the general election. That’s huge.

“Let’s put it to Westminster and put the onus on them to meet us at the table and set that plan out for us.”

The latest MRP polling by Electoral Calculus this week predicted a narrow Labour victory , with the SNP winning 28 seats, although previous polls have indicated they could win even more.

In a visit to Lanarkshire on Friday, the prime minister, Andy Burnham, said the Scottish government needed to “move beyond” the question of independence while offering to work more closely on devolving power from Holyrood with Swinney’s administration. The Westminster government would have to grant a second vote on Scottish independence.

“I just feel we all have to move beyond the constitutional questions. In my view, people in Scotland are suffering the cost of living crisis, like they are in England and everywhere else. And I think our job is to focus on the practicalities, to focus on solutions for people. Right now, too much time is wasted on those dramas. It consumes too much energy,” he said, when asked about the issue.

Although it is not in Swinney’s power to call a second independence referendum, he told the conference that another vote could happen sooner than expected.

“Our independence is very close,” he said. “Our nearest neighbours will always be our closest friends and our strongest allies. I will always want the very best for the people living in England, Wales and across Ireland.

“But friends, in the long arc of history, nothing is static. And those that try to hold on to the past fail to grasp the opportunities of the future.

“In this period of history, the nations of the United Kingdom are evolving into a new relationship. That is something to welcome.”

items.lbText:
Ukrainian president warns it will embolden Russian leader and intensify war as Moscow hits country’s power plants

Power plant attacks reflect Russian blueprint to make Ukrainian cities unlivable

Volodymyr Zelenskyy has described Donald Trump’s decision to roll back sanctions on Russia as a “reward” for Vladimir Putin and warned it will embolden the Russian leader and intensify the Kremlin’s war, as Moscow launched one of its worst strikes yet on Ukraine’s power plants in an attempt to black out the country’s cities before winter.

The Ukrainian president also said he expected the Trump administration to lift more sanctions against Russia in the future and called for Europe to establish its own negotiations with Moscow as the US has sought better ties and business deals with the Kremlin.

“Unfortunately, the lifting of sanctions will continue, and I believe that the ‘diesel deal’ is the first step,” said Zelenskyy on Saturday. “Unfortunately, it seems to me that this cannot stop Putin; on the contrary, he feels joy and happiness that he has such support.”

In a social media message earlier, Zelenskyy wrote: “A US ⁠sanctions blackout, easing pressure on the aggressor, financial rewards for Putin – all of this only encourages him to keep attacking. We must not give up ground.

“We must keep trying to end the ‌war. To end it, not give Putin every reason to continue it indefinitely.”

In its latest effort to reduce tensions with Russia , Trump announced on Friday that he would put a hold on a sweeping new sanctions package targeting the Russian economy, telling Congress the pause on the legislation passed by both chambers was in the national interest.

The act, named for the late senator Lindsey Graham, who championed the legislation , would have introduced tough new sanctions on Russia including a 100% tariff on major importers of Russian oil such as China and India, as well as sanctions on Russia’s energy sector, financial institutions and shadow fleet of oil tankers.

On Saturday, Zelenskyy said the decision to waive the sanctions would encourage Vladimir Putin to intensify the war in Ukraine and called for support in the US to resurrect the bill.

“At the time when the Russians launched such a massive strike against our energy sector, in America, regrettably, a decision was made to completely ignore the Lindsey Graham law, which was supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia to end this war,” he wrote in a statement. “This law could have – and still can! – help a great deal. But the law needs to actually work, and every voice in support of it matters.”

The move was greeted by the Russian presidential envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, who wrote on social media: “The Trump administration’s suspension of the Graham Act is an important and truly historic moment.”

The legislation, which sanctions Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers that keeps the country’s energy supplies moving, was due to be implemented in two days.

It also directs Trump to impose up to 100% tariffs on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia’s natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports.

Friday’s announcement comes a week after Trump said the US had agreed to purchase diesel from Russia to try to bring down global energy prices, upending years of US and western pressure on the Kremlin to end its war against Ukraine.

Trump said last week that Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tonnes in November and 1m tonnes “immediately thereafter”. Russia would deliver an additional 3m tonnes “within a short period of time” after that, he wrote.

The Trump administration’s decision to waive the sanctions is the latest consequence of a brutal quarrel between Trump and Zelenskyy. Several times this week, the US did not provide intelligence of impending ballistic missile attacks to Ukraine , and the White House reportedly ordered the Pentagon to throttle the military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet network used by Ukraine’s armed forces to run its drone operations on the frontline.

“We very much hope – and I personally hope – that the president of the United States of America will do everything so that Putin stops the killings, stops the strikes on our energy infrastructure, and stops this war,” Zelenskyy said on Saturday. “But once again, you cannot achieve this by restricting Ukraine’s responses to Russia for killing our people. And even less so by lifting sanctions.”

Trump has demanded that Ukraine halt its strikes on Russian oil refineries, as he has blamed the war in Ukraine, rather than the closure of the strait of Hormuz, for the worldwide spike in diesel prices. Ukraine unilaterally halted the strikes after Trump declared an “energy ceasefire” last week, but resumed them when it became clear that Russia was stepping up its attacks on Ukrainian power plants and substations.

Zelenskyy said on Saturday that Russia had launched one of its worst strikes yet against the country’s energy infrastructure, hitting more than 15 critical power generation and transmission facilities and causing “severe consequences”.

He also indicated that Ukraine’s dwindling stock of anti-air weapons made it difficult to shoot down many of the loitering munitions, cruise missiles and ballistic missiles being launched each night at Ukraine.

“Although our warriors are shooting down a significant number of them,” he said, the “sheer scale and unrelenting pace of Russia’s strikes, specifically against our energy sector, are unfortunately having severe consequences.”

items.title: Pope Leo discharged from hospital after cancer operation
items.author: Angela Giuffrida in Rome
items.content:
Doctors say pontiff is ‘fit for discharge’ after operation to remove cancerous tumour from his lung

Leo, 71, was deemed “fit for discharge”, his doctors, Luigi Carbone and Stefano Margaritora, said in a statement published by the Vatican.

Continue reading...
items.lbText:
Doctors say pontiff is ‘fit for discharge’ after operation to remove cancerous tumour from his lung

Pope Leo lung cancer surgery: what kind of operation did he have and what happens next?

Pope Leo has been discharged from hospital in Rome after undergoing an operation to remove a cancerous tumour from his lung .

Leo, 71, was deemed “fit for discharge”, his doctors, Luigi Carbone and Stefano Margaritora, said in a statement published by the Vatican.

He walked unaided from the hospital on Saturday afternoon, to cheers from well-wishers.

Leo, who in May last year became the first US-born leader of the Roman Catholic church, has been in the Gemelli hospital since Tuesday, when doctors removed part of his right lung in order to extract the tumour.

“Considering the blood tests, the chest X-ray done this morning, and evaluating the clinical picture, the Holy Father has been deemed fit for discharge,” the statement said.

Doctors said on Wednesday that Leo’s recovery from the operation was progressing normally. They are waiting for the results of tests to determine whether the cancer has spread and if more treatment will be needed.

Leo was diagnosed with the most common kind of lung cancer – adenocarcinoma.

The pontiff celebrated mass in his room on the 10th-floor of the Gemelli hospital in the north-west of the Italian capital before being discharged.

The Vatican said he would recite the Angelus prayer on Sunday “from the window of the papal apartment”. It was during his angelus last week, in a rare moment of Vatican transparency, that Leo made the shock announcement to the crowd gathered in St Peter’s Square that a small nodule on his lung had been detected during a check-up.

The pope has worked from hospital, including making a phone call on Friday to Vladimir Putin, during which he urged the Russian president to call a ceasefire in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky.

The Vatican had originally estimated a week-long stay in hospital. The pope’s appointments had been cancelled until 20 October.

It is uncertain if he’ll make an intense 12-day trip to South America planned in November.

Cardinal ​Pietro Parolin, the Vatican’s secretary of state, told reporters on Friday that Leo may need to readjust his trip schedule, at least with regard to South America, depending on his health.

Before the cancer diagnosis, Leo, who enjoys sports, especially playing tennis, was generally believed to be in good health. He often makes use of the papal retreat in Castel Gandolfo, close to Rome.

The Gemelli, located in the north-west of the Italian capital, is renowned for treating reigning popes. Pope John Paul II stayed there so many times that the Vatican worked with the hospital to establish a high-security papal suite.

The Chilean-American author Isabel Allende has won Spain’s €1m (£843,000) Premio Planeta, one of the world’s most lucrative literary prizes, under a pseudonym, with a sequel to her celebrated debut novel, The House of the Spirits.

Allende, 84, won the 75th edition of the award on Thursday with La hora antes del alba , which returns to the characters of her 1982 novel, a multigenerational family saga set against political upheaval in a country inspired by Chile .

The new story follows Alba, the granddaughter of Esteban Trueba and Clara del Valle, as she tries to recover from imprisonment and torture during Pinochet’s dictatorship, according to Reuters. Allende said the book would bring the universe of The House of the Spirits to a close. The 1982 novel is often read alongside Daughter of Fortune and Portrait in Sepia as part of a loose trilogy of interconnected family sagas.

Speaking at the award ceremony in Barcelona, attended by King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia, Allende said it was “like winning the Nobel”.

“I had never entered a competition because I wanted to avoid the embarrassment of coming last,” she said. “At my age, there is very little to lose.”

She said she had been prompted to write the sequel by decades of readers asking what happened to Alba. She also drew parallels between the political circumstances surrounding the novel and the contemporary rise of extremism. Allende was forced into exile after the 1973 military coup led by Augusto Pinochet that overthrew the Chilean president Salvador Allende, a cousin of her father. Allende had been Latin America’s first democratically elected Marxist leader. Under Pinochet’s regime, an estimated 40,000 people were tortured and more than 3,000 killed.

“Now that I see so many democracies threatened by authoritarianism, extreme nationalism and even fascism, I feel again the fear that led me to leave my country,” she said.

Allende is one of the best-known writers in the Spanish-speaking world, whose books have sold more than 80m copies worldwide and been translated into more than 40 languages. The prize is open to unpublished manuscripts, with the option of submitting under a pseudonym, and Allende entered under the name Luz Ventura, with the fictional title Los que faltan .

However, the judges may have been able to pick up on Allende’s style. “I’d be very surprised if the judges did not know that it was Isabel Allende,” said Prof Duncan Wheeler, the chair of Spanish studies at Leeds University and president-elect of the Association of Hispanists of Great Britain and Ireland. “You have to bear in mind that the Planeta prize is one of the most generously remunerated in the Spanish-speaking world, but definitely not the most prestigious.”

The prize has at times faced criticism over the choice of winner. In 2021, the prize was awarded to La bestia , a thriller published under the pseudonym Carmen Mola, which had been marketed as the identity of a female author. At the awards ceremony, it was revealed that Mola was in fact three male writers – Jorge Díaz, Agustín Martínez and Antonio Mercero.

The prize is run by Planeta, one of the largest publishing groups in the Spanish-speaking world, and includes the condition that the winning book be published by them. Allende has been published by Plaza & Janés, an imprint of Penguin Random House, since The House of the Spirits, so this marks a significant coup for Planeta.

Despite the option to submit pseudonymously, the prize has a history of favouring established writers and TV figures: past winners of the prize have included prominent Spanish-language authors such as Juan Marsé and Manuel Vázquez Montalbán, and the controversial TV personality Juan de Val.

Asked about the perceived trend of awarding the prize to figures known for appearing on TV shows, José Creuheras, the president of the Planeta Group, said, according to the Spanish newspaper El País: “I’m not in a position to say whether the Planeta Prize has more or less prestige than it did in the past. We have some of contemporary literature’s biggest names among our winners and finalists. The prize’s reach, as measured by the figures, speaks for itself, and the number of people taking an interest in the Planeta is growing.”

The runner-up was the Spanish writer and screenwriter Sergio Hernández, whose historical novel La añoranza won €200,000.

items.lbText:
School looking to sell piece of open land beloved by people in Devon town to fund refurbishments

On Saturdays throughout autumn, residents of Totnes have met at a field on the banks of the River Dart to play ballgames, fly kites or simply sit on the grass and chat.

But it hasn’t just been about having fun – this has been a “play protest” aimed at trying to save a beloved piece of open land in the historic Devon market town.

The local comprehensive, King Edward VI Community College (KEVICC) , has been given the go-ahead by the UK government to sell the 1.5-hectare plot – Lower Field – and it is likely houses will be built on it.

School leaders say they desperately need funds to revamp neglected buildings but campaigners claim the sell-off is an example of land that has been used by communities for decades being whisked away – a modern “enclosure” of public space.

“It’s devastating,” said Becca Robinson, who uses the field for women’s and girls’ fitness classes. “I’m trying to get women and girls to be more active and to get outdoors. The great thing about the field is it’s an open space, so it feels safe. It really worries me that, if we lost it, fewer women and girls will exercise.

“It’s also a spot people go just to do their own thing rather than take part in structured sport. You can just make an ad hoc decision to go and play a game or just to sit and read.”

Earlier this year, the anti-poverty charity Trussell published research revealing almost half of UK residents (45%) had lost access to at least one community space – such as a park, social club, library or post office – since 2023.

Danielle McIlven, who has been organising games of rounders on the field, attended the school and said Lower Field had been part of her life for years. “It’s about the unstructured play that can take place there. In the summer you see swarms of teenagers playing there or heading down to the river.”

Anna Ali, the organiser of a women’s football “kickabout” and a member of the campaign group Friends of Lower Field , said the town had a reputation for being middle class and affluent. “But there is quite a lot of hidden impoverishment. Public green spaces are vital. I was speaking to a woman who brings her grandchildren here. They can’t afford to join sports clubs, so kicking a ball around on the field is a lifeline.”

Lewis Winks, a leading member of the Right to Roam group, said Lower Field had been shared by the school and the wider Totnes community since it was gifted by the Elmhirst family, known for progressive farming, forestry and educational projects on the nearby Dartington Estate , about a century ago.

A key issue the Friends group is digging into is the details of the Elmhirst gift – and whether it may have been legally given to the community or permanently protected for community use.

Winks said: “Lower Field is a vital place for young people and families to play, exercise and spend time together. Losing it would undermine the town’s vitality and wellbeing.”

The Friends group wants Education South West, the trust the school is part of, to explore whether the field could be sold to the community. Winks said: “We are asking for a realistic window to raise the money. A community purchase could help fund improvements at KEVICC while safeguarding the field for its pupils and the wider community.”

But it is a race against time. The land is expected to be put on the market in January, giving little time to raise funds. Campaigners also highlight that measures under the English Devolution and Community Empowerment Act 2026 aimed at giving communities greater influence over the places and assets that matter to them are unlikely to come into force in time. “We’re falling through the gap regarding a right to buy,” Winks said.

Matthew Shanks, chief executive of Education South West , said it understood how important the site was to the Totnes community and wanted to have an open and constructive conversation with people.

He said money raised would support significant refurbishment and modernisation across the school estate, including improvements to buildings and facilities. Shanks said the school would retain playing fields which would remain available for public use.

School principal Alan Salt said he understood the future of the field mattered hugely to the community. “We want to be open and transparent about what is proposed.” The trust and school have organised an open meeting to discuss the field.

Salt argued that selling it made sound financial sense. There had been little capital investment in the school for six years and it had “temporary” classrooms more than half a century old.

“So we’ve got a really acute set of challenges within a very difficult national context,” he said. “At the end of the day, we are a comprehensive school trying to get the best for the students in a really difficult national picture.”
